articles.headline: The Cow-Boy's Tale.
articles.text:
"Are there no real good Injuns?"
The cow-boy raised his head,
And glancing at the tenderfoot,
He turned to him and said:
"I rode the prairies, pardner,
Ten years in rain and sun,
But as to 'real good Injuns,'
I haven't met more nor one,
A swig o' that hoss liniment,
And then I'll try to place
This A 1 virtuous redskin
That for goodness trumped the ace,
'Twas at the bar at Mack's Ford,
A lot o' boys one day
Got to making things quite lively
In a ball and cartridge way,
I banged around about me,
And didn't count the odds—
I'd been soaking electricity
Like fifty lightning rods:
When suddenly the sheriff
And his gang came bounding down,
And the boys took to their cattle
And dusted outen town.
But suthin' was the matter
With my head works, I dare say,
For I stumbled by the roadside,
And I couldn't find my way;
And the next I can remember,
It was night, and pitchy black,
And I tried to strike the trail from there,
But couldn't hit a track,
And I was mighty dizzy
And felt I should have died,
When standing just before,
An Injun's shape I spied,
He held his hands out to me,
But I didn't say a word;
And when I tried to hail him,
He neither spoke nor stirred,
And then I slipped in somehow
Between each sturdy arm,
And then he let me down so gently,
Without a bit o' harm;
And I lay there quite contented,
And slept until 'twas day,
And woke to find him watching
At my side the same old way;
So I climbed upon my uprights,
And a word I couldn't say,
But I looked the red man in the face,
And then I sneaked away.
We parted. But, as years passed by,
I wonder more and more
If still that real good Injun stands
At Mack's tobacco store."
—[The Northwest.
articles.summary: Humorous verse, credited to The Northwest, in which a cowboy's 'real good Injun' turns out to be a cigar-store Indian.

articles.text:
The weakest article of all the maudlin trash that has appeared against our freight route emanated from a Dickinson numskull and was published in the Pioneer-Press of the 14th. The article says: "We claim, and with justice, that the best road to that point (Deadwood) is from Dickinson." How does this sound when taken in connection with the statement of The Dickinson Press that a committee was appointed to view the road as soon as practicable? The article goes on to say: "We claim, also, that this is the proper place from which to ship the freight, as it is the end of the Missouri freight division of the railroad." Does the writer have any idea that a railroad in such a case as this looks at the "proper" side of the case? A railroad is built and run to make money. The Northern Pacific can make more money by having a freight route start[?] from this point. Ergo, it will start from here. The article adds to the above quotation that to have the route start from here "will necessitate the expenditure of vast sums of money by the railroad company for additional side-tracks, freight houses, etc." Were this even a fact, a practical view of the matter settles it. If it pays the railroad company to go to any additional expense they will do it, otherwise they will not. The fact of the matter is, however, that the Marquis de Mores stands all the expense of extra buildings, and if the freight route had never been thought of, our growing trade would have compelled the railroad company to put in a side-track.

The article further states: "The road from Little Missouri (or Medora, as it is now called) is through an almost impassable series of buttes or Bad Lands." The writer here displays his ignorance of even the starting point of our route and states a willful lie in reference to the road in the Bad Lands. We call the lie willful because no writer has any business describing a thing of which his own utterances display his utter ignorance. We would willingly pay our share toward the expenses of an unbiased committee to view the merits of the two roads. Our road is as level as a floor and will not need a bridge, and only a little grading in one place while in the Bad Lands. The writer is informed that our road is decided upon. The road which their committee will "view as soon as practicable" he is, of course, as ignorant of as he is of ours. For his benefit we will state that the road from Dickinson that is free from gumbo consists of what are called "buffalo wallows." That is, there is a space, say of ten feet, where the ground is as bare as a floor. Then comes an equal space of turf about six inches higher than the general level. In the lightest buggy it is impossible to go over this land on a trot. With heavy freight wagons the jar will be sufficient to tear the horses' shoulders to pieces. Also, Mr. Ignorance, we would like to know if you have figured on "the vast sums of money" it will take to bridge your route? Of course, you haven't, for your committee has not yet found it practicable to view your route.

But right here is where the most laughable ignorance of this writer is displayed. The very thing which condemns the Dickinson route beyond all peradventure. He says their route "crosses the head-waters of the North and South Cannonball rivers, the Grand river (north and south forks)" and then goes further out of his way to condemn the route by saying that "it crosses a number of small streams known by various names, whereas the more western route from Little Missouri heads some of them, thus missing a number of watering places." We should say our route did "miss some of the watering places." Almost from the Heart river to the South Moreau on the Dickinson route is one vast "watering place." But we never heard gumbo called a "watering place" before.

The rest of the article is a mass of drivel that only reminds one of a spoiled child blubbering because a valuable toy that it does not know how to handle has been taken away from it. And, now, we want to ask this writer of what good was his production? If any one wants a freight route they must work for it personally. A mass of rot such as this article is can do nothing but injury. The falsity of most of the statements and the pusillanimity of the rest condemn the article as the route is already condemned. We dislike to fight men of straw such as the writer of this article has proved himself to be, as it scarcely furnishes the needed exercise. For the good of Dickinson we hope this effervescent individual will be effectually corkedup or he may slop over again.
articles.summary: Packard attacks a Dickinson writer in the Pioneer-Press of the 14th who claimed the Black Hills freight route should start at Dickinson, defending the Medora route.

articles.headline: EGOTISTICAL.
articles.text:
Following a time-honored custom with newspapers we publish below a few of the many favorable comments we have received at the hands of the press. We don't believe much in a paper blowing its own trumpet, but like crumpets, we find these extracts "werry filin' at the price."

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY is the name of a new paper in Little Missouri, Dak., and is owned and edited by A. T. Packard, '83. We are in receipt of the first two numbers and they look as newsy and neat as though printed in a city printing house and not a thousand miles from nowhere. "Pack" can run a paper as well as he can curve a base-ball and no fears for the new sheet need be entertained.—[Ann Arbor, Mich., University Chronicle.

A handsome, wide-awake weekly paper called THE BAD LANDS COW BOY has been started at Medora, formerly Little Missouri, Dak., by A. T. Packard. It will have a good field in representing the cattle and sheep industries of one of the best grazing regions of the West, and in chronicling the growth and doings of the new town founded by the Marquis de Mores.—[The Northwest.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY of which A. T. Packard, a former Chicago reporter, is the editor, tells each of the 600 what the rest have been doing during the week, and to the public at large details the many natural and acquired advantages of the new city as a place of business and residence. It has done this since February 4, a day that will therefore long be remembered in Medora.—[New York Sun.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, a new newspaper published at Little Missouri has reached our table. It is filled with fresh news and is of neat makeup. THE COW BOY is published in the heart of the Bad Lands of Western Dakota which are becoming famous as the best stock ranges in this country, if not in the world, and will devote considerable of its space to the stock industry.—[Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.

This week brings to our editorial table the initial number of THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, published by A. T. Packard, Medora, Dak., not for fun (as he says) but whereby to make a living. The paper starts out well, and we trust will keep up its lick, as The Northwestern Live Stock Journal (the daddy of all stock journals in the Northwest) wishes to see its children succeed. THE COW BOY is a four-page, seven-column paper, ably edited and representing well the interest for which mission it has started in.—[Cheyenne, Wyo., Northwestern Live Stock Journal.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, published at Little Missouri, Dak., is a surprisingly good paper.—[Minneapolis Hotel Register.

The first issue of THE BAD LAND COW BOY, published by A. T. Packard, at Little Missouri, is full of interesting matter to stock men. It aims to be the best cattle paper in the Northwest, and we trust the long-felt want among the ranchmen is filled by this paper.—[Dickinson Press.

Little Missouri has a newspaper which sails under the significant name of THE BAD LANDS COW BOY. Typographically it is excellent. It is ably edited by A. T. Packard.—[Glendive Times.

THE BAD LANDS COW BOY is the unique title of a thorough cattle paper, published at Medora, Dak., which is fast becoming a noted cattle point. It gives all the cattle and general news of the Bad Lands and advocates Medora as the cattle headquarters of the Northwest. The name of the paper calls attention to the two things concerning which the editor, A. T. Packard wishes to change public opinion, as the Bad Lands are not bad but very good and produce mints of money; and the cowboys, as a rule, are good citizens. The exceptions have formed public opinion against them.—[Pioneer-Press.
articles.summary: Reprints favorable notices of The Cow Boy from nine other newspapers.

articles.headline: ON THE RANGE.
articles.text:
The Cattle buyers of Eastern Washington Territory are paying $12 for calves, $18 for yearlings, $25 for two-year-olds and $40 for cows.—Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.

A correspondent writing from LaCueva, Mora Co., N. M., says: "Cattle in this part of the country are fat enough to ship. I hear of considerable losses in Colfax county, north of this, and also out on the other side of Red river.

Yearling steers are worth from $11.50 to $12.50 and twos from $14.50 to $17. We refer to steer cattle. Better classes of yearlings sell from $12 up. Beeves are in good demand, but scarce at any price, if fat.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

E. E. Crawford, Miles City, Mont., writes: "Stock of all kinds has wintered well thus far. On the range the horses and native cattle are fat; state cattle, late arrivals last fall, are a little thin. Loss, nothing to speak of. Unless we should have some very rough weather this month they will pull through all right."

The winter is over, if we know ourselves. Warm weather and the grass-growing rains have blessed a large portion of the country and the prospect is good. Our correspondents refer to the last spell of weather, which was threatening bad, but let up easily. Texas stock, on the average, wintered exceedingly well.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped range news on cattle prices and wintering in Washington Territory, New Mexico, Montana and Texas.

articles.text:
We notice many papers of late printing the names of parties prominent in rounding up cattle crooks. This is not advisable. The thieves know who are hunting them and keep out of the way. It exposes stock detectives and parties assisting to unnecessary danger. Thief-takers are not grateful for gratuitous advertising of their business.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

One of the largest sales of property ever made in the far west took place Friday, by which the Swan Land and Cattle Company purchased for a consideration of $2,588,825 upward of 88,000 head of cattle, besides ranch improvements, horses and other kinds of personal property and immense tracts of land, all of said property being in this county.—[Cheyenne Sun.

Mr. F. P. Ernest sometime last season bought a bunch of cattle of the Prairie Cattle Company, in the southern part of the state. Without handling a beef or looking at a single animal he had purchased, Mr. Ernest sold the cattle to the outfit known as the Mill-Iron Company, which was formerly the John Hitson Company, at an advance over the purchase of $32,000.—[Pueblo, Colo., Chieftain.

There was, perhaps, never a brighter outlook for the stock interests of Texas than at present. The nippers have been prohibited, made a deadly weapon, so to speak, the stock have wintered in good shape, those who have no land are arranging to secure it, those who have land are fencing or preparing to fence it, and, indeed, it begins to look as if the new era in the stock business of Texas, that we have been all along predicting, is about to be ushered in.—[Texas Stockmen.

Fifteen years ago people who had small herds of cattle, and when the state did not contain more than 100,000 head, proclaimed the thing overdone, and wanted the gates closed. They said there was room for no more. But despite this discouragement the increase has gone on until now we have 1,500,000 and there is room for more. Five years from now there will be as many cattle grazed west of the Continental Divide as there are east of it at the present time.—[Colorado Live Stock Record.

Plenty of food and enough exercise to keep the muscles firm is the best treatment of horses in winter. It is quite common for many farmers to underfeed in winter, because they have little or nothing for horses to do. But a horse thus managed soon loses his capacity for hard service. Such a horse may be fed so as to make a good show in spring, but it will be fat, not muscle, and a few days in plowing or harrowing will bring him down. Horses worked continuously are less liable to [gall?] from the harness, as the skin is always firm and hard.—[Journal of Agriculture.

Mr. Bennett, who is employed by the Colorado Cattle Growers' Association to inspect the cattle killed by the railroads, is just in from Wallace, Kan., and reports large numbers of Republican river cattle suffering and dying on account of the large pasture fences on North Smoky river. These cattle are dying on both the outside and inside of the pastures. On the outside they die from want of water. Some hundreds of them have broken through the fence to get water, and the pastures having all been eaten out last fall and the cattle that were in them turned out south before winter set in, leaves them on the inside with no grass and they are dying in as great numbers as those on the outside.—[Denver Republican.

Effective measures have already been taken to prevent the spread of the foot and mouth disease in Kansas. Gov. Glick, himself a large cattle owner, is personally interesting himself in the matter and a strict quarantine has been effected. The disease has undoubtedly spread from cattle that have been imported. Hereafter it is probable that the health of all imported stock will be strictly inquired into. The disease itself is a very contagious eruptive fever. It is communicable not only between animals of the same species but between those of species entirely different. For instance, it spreads from cattle to sheep, pigs and fowls and vice versa. The symptoms according to Prof. Law are, roughness of the coat or shivering, increased temperature, dry muzzle, hot red mouth, teats, and interdigital spaces, lameness, inclination to lie and shrinking from the hand in milking. The second or third day blisters arise on any part of the whole interior of the mouth, one-half to one inch in breadth, or on the teats and digits about one-half inch across. Saliva drivels from the mouth, collecting in froth around the lips and a loud smacking is made with the lips and tongue. Swine champ the jaws. Sheep and swine suffer more especially in the feet, often losing the hoofs or even the digital bones, a contingency not unknown in neglected cattle. We do not need to enter into a description of the prevention and cure of this disease, as it will probably never trouble any of our cattle men. It is sufficient to say that the quarantine is so effective that it is not at all likely to spread out of the five or six miles of infected district in Kansas.
articles.summary: Clipped stock news from other papers: cattle-thief reporting, the Swan Land and Cattle Company sale, Texas and Colorado outlooks, horse care, Kansas pasture die-off and foot and mouth quarantine.

articles.summary: Plug for the Far West cigar at Roberts & Co.

articles.text: In this climate and weather it is sufficient enjoyment to exist.
articles.summary: Remark on the pleasant weather.

articles.text: The dance at the Hotel de Mores Monday night was a very pleasant affair.
articles.summary: A dance at the Hotel de Mores on Monday night was a pleasant affair.

articles.text: The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
articles.summary: The Senate holds the sole agency for the Far West cigar.

articles.text: Gill Kennedy went to Belfield Saturday. He has a claim adjoining the townsite.
articles.summary: Gill Kennedy went to Belfield, where he has a claim adjoining the townsite.

articles.text: The Marquis started for St. Paul the 17th and will doubtless be here inside of a week.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores left for St. Paul on the 17th and is expected back within a week.

articles.text: J. M. Cook sold his team and outfit Tuesday, to A. T. Packard, to be used on the butte farm.
articles.summary: J. M. Cook sold his team and outfit to A. T. Packard for the butte farm.

articles.text: Will McNaughton, running for Dan Eisenberg, of Bismarck, put in a profitable day here last Saturday.
articles.summary: Will McNaughton, travelling for Dan Eisenberg of Bismarck, did good business in town Saturday.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific bridge gang went up the road Monday. The pile-driver will soon start on its spring trip.
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific bridge gang went up the road Monday.

articles.text: Abe Goodkind, travelling for Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, was in town Saturday. He had good success here.
articles.summary: Abe Goodkind of Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, was in town Saturday.

articles.text: Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
articles.summary: Wise & Goodkind gave Roberts & Co. sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.

articles.text: "Doc" Pennell has gone to Deadwood via the Medora route. Part or all of Mr. Jones' teams will doubtless return with him.
articles.summary: "Doc" Pennell has gone to Deadwood via the Medora route.

articles.text: C. A. Williams, of Bismarck, was in the city yesterday. He showed his appreciation of THE COW BOY by subscribing and advertising.
articles.summary: C. A. Williams of Bismarck visited and subscribed and advertised.

articles.text: Pennell & Roberts drove their transportation outfit in from their ranch last Saturday and went into camp south of the railroad track.
articles.summary: Pennell & Roberts brought their transportation outfit in and camped south of the track.

articles.text: The latest reports from all along the river for fifty miles up state that the cattle are in prime condition, many being fat enough to kill.
articles.summary: Reports say cattle for fifty miles up the river are in prime condition.

articles.text: Only two head of the Marquis' cattle have died this winter. These were pure-bred Durhams that died from accidents. Out of about fifteen hundred head this is a splendid showing.
articles.summary: Only two of the Marquis' roughly 1,500 cattle died over the winter.

articles.text: Johnny Goodall, Frank Smith and Rev. Silas Cheval are the latest contributors to our Bad Lands museum. The latter "held up" a passing freight and secured a good specimen of galena.
articles.summary: Johnny Goodall, Frank Smith and Rev. Silas Cheval contributed specimens to the Bad Lands museum.

articles.text: Moody and Jones, of the "Big Foot" Ryder outfit came in for supplies this week. When not "tired" they reported 5,000 posts cut. The increase, however, was about 1,000 posts to the "smile."
articles.summary: Moody and Jones of the "Big Foot" Ryder outfit came in for supplies and reported 5,000 posts cut.

articles.text: Howard Eaton will probably have the largest barn in the county when it is finished. It is a "ready-made" barn, every piece being cut to fit its proper place. Several teams are busy hauling the parts to Howard's ranch.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton is putting up a ready-made barn, probably the largest in the county.

articles.text: If any one doubts that the cattle are in good condition, let them go to the company's meat market or cold-storage room here and look at the cattle slaughtered Tuesday. They are rolling in fat and have had nothing to eat but the grass they rustled.
articles.summary: Cattle slaughtered Tuesday at the company's market were fat from grass alone.

articles.text: The river was on a big boom Monday. A gorge forming a few miles up the river and breaking about 12 o'clock. For two or three hours it was a grand sight to see the broken ice shoot down stream. The current for a while was fully twelve miles an hour.
articles.summary: An ice gorge broke on the Little Missouri on Monday, sending ice down at twelve miles an hour.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific, in connection with the new fast mail from New York to Chicago and St. Paul, will soon change their time from St. Paul to Portland to ninety-two hours instead of one hundred and four. The trains will then run through the Bad Lands in daylight, and two each way will be put on probably the first of the month.
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific will cut St. Paul-Portland time to ninety-two hours, running through the Bad Lands in daylight.

articles.text: Work is progressing in good shape on the Packard-Steiger butte farm. As soon as the frost is out of the ground, plowing will commence. All sorts of vegetables will be planted to see which will do the best. The most of the ground, however, will be planted with potatoes. It will be an interesting experiment to find out what the summits of the buttes are good for.
articles.summary: Work progresses on the Packard-Steiger butte farm, to be planted mostly in potatoes.

articles.text: Reduced rates on emigrant movables have been issued by the Northern Pacific R. R. The term "emigrant movables" is meant to apply to any part of the outfit of an intending settler. This includes second-hand household goods, farming implements and tools and vehicles, trees, shrubbery, fowls and not to exceed ten head of live stock per car. It does not include merchandise, provisions, grain (except for feed in transit and fifty bushels for seed), or any article intended for sale. Twenty-five hundred feet of lumber and 500 fence posts, and portable houses may also be shipped. The rates are proportionate for any amount and are $71 per car of 20,000 pounds from St. Paul to Little Missouri.
articles.summary: The Northern Pacific issued reduced rates on emigrant movables, $71 per car from St. Paul to Little Missouri.

articles.text: John Doulisch met with a serious accident yesterday. He was excavating the dirt next to Michael Knott's saloon for a new building, when a number of large lumps fell on him. Joe Pennell and two or three others happened to be passing and stopped on hearing the noise. A slight groan convinced them that some one was hurt, but nothing could be seen except the frozen blocks of displaced earth. It took the combined strength of three men to roll the blocks off of Doulisch. It is not thought that he has received any internal injury, but it is difficult to tell at present. He was resting much easier last night. The victim would not have lived five minutes had he not been relieved from the pressure as he was squeezed so hard that it was impossible for him to breathe.
articles.summary: John Doulisch was nearly crushed by frozen earth while excavating next to Michael Knott's saloon.

articles.headline: Contributed.
articles.text:
Let dogs delight to bark and bite,
For God hath made them so;
Let bears and lions growl and fight,
For 'tis their nature too.

But, Sandy, you should never let
Your angry passions rise,
Your hands were never made
To scratch out Jones' eyes.
articles.summary: Contributed verse, a parody of Isaac Watts addressed to "Sandy," warning against scratching out Jones' eyes.

articles.headline: Round-Up Meeting.
articles.text: Messrs. Boice and Towers arrived in town this afternoon to make arrangements for a round-up meeting to be held in Pennell's Hall, Little Missouri, April 5. This notice will take the place of a call, as enough cattle men are already interested to insure the success of the meeting. Turn out, stockmen.
articles.summary: Boice and Towers arrived to arrange a stockmen's round-up meeting at Pennell's Hall, Little Missouri, April 5.

articles.headline: The Medora Freight Route.
articles.text:
The latest thing in reference to the freight route is that the Northwestern and Milwaukee roads have pooled and lowered rates to meet the Rock Island schedule. These rates apply to Medora, Dickinson and Belfield. Every town has a fair show and that is all our route wants. On account of the superiority of our road, none other can possibly compete with it.

In reply to our "preposterous remarks about the freight line," the Press claims that it is not a fact that freight now in Dickinson is to be shipped here and freighted from this point. Up to date, this is the first "claim" emanating from Dickinson that is substantiated by facts. We were misled into stating it by reading orders from Messrs. Jansen & Bliss, Blum, Zeipp and F. B. Smith, of Deadwood, for all freight at Dickinson to be turned over to Cranston; also orders from Cranston to turn over the freight to Jones & Pennell. Upon inquiry, however, it was found that there was only a car-load or two at Dickinson and the firm here wouldn't ship such a small amount, and this very freight that we don't want is what Dickinson has gone so wild over!

The Press further states that eleven loaded freight outfits had started for the Black Hills last week. Your vocabulary needs enlarging, Bro. Scott. In speaking of outfits, one does not call every team an outfit. Mr. Jones' outfit will haul 200,000 pounds, Pennell & Roberts' 100,000 and Larson's 75,000.

The Press goes on to say:

"We will now give the facts as they exist at the present time. Keyes & Bramble, heavy freighters, have made contracts with the railroad to have all of their freight delivered at Dickinson and at no other point. Jones & Pennell have made contracts to have their freight delivered either at Dickinson or Little Missouri."

As food for thought on the part of The Press we will "give the facts" in the shape of a telegram from Mr. Jones to Mr. Pennell:

DEADWOOD, March 16, 1884.
JOE PENNELL, Little Missouri, Dak.:
Have made contracts with many merchants. Have consolidated with Bramble in favor of Medora route. (Signed) JONES.

Read, Bro. Scott, and then go out and weep a spring freshet into the Heart river.
articles.summary: Rebuts the Dickinson Press on the Black Hills freight route, printing a telegram from Jones in Deadwood that he has consolidated with Bramble in favor of the Medora route.

articles.headline: BELFIELD GOSSIP.
articles.text:
BELFIELD, Dak., March 19, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

Belfield is much pleased with the efforts of THE COW BOY in urging prompt organization of the county. Billings county is one of the richest of Dakota and for its age, most densely populated. We are entitled to organization and the executive should recognize the fact.

Two dozen buttons came off when the Dickinson freight-line article was read in The Pioneer-Press.

Will Houk celebrated his twenty-third birthday on Sunday last, and hilarity reigned supreme upon this festive occasion.

The Galliens, who were expected to return last week, have not arrived yet and it is feared that their little child, which was sick at St. Paul, has grown worse.

The first new settler, Mr. Schurke, of Chicago, arrived last Monday, and will be followed by six families within a week.

The snow is disappearing fast and it is beginning to be unsafe to venture through the many creeks with ordinary ponies.

Quite a traffic in relinquishment papers has commenced here. Many excellent claims were filed on by speculators last season who are now trying to unload. Such proceedings are utterly unlawful and suggest food for a special agent of the U. S. land department.

Quite a number of Indians passed through here a few days ago.

A somewhat interesting case of horse stealing came to light this week. A party of Indians recognized among some ponies belonging to our citizens, one which they claimed had been stolen from them three years ago and were going to take it from their present owner. After considerable parleying they were induced to seek redress by legal process, and will likely recover their animal to-day. The pony has passed through three different hands here and was originally purchased from the Townsite Company for $60. The moral attached to this item is that no one should ever purchase any kind of stock without taking a bill of sale for his money, or run the risk of being arrested for horse stealing.

Boomer Kennedy was down from Little Missouri this week and thinks of erecting a two-story store this season.

Senor Bass, the Delmonico of Billings county, entertained a number of guests royally on St. Patrick's day.

The anniversary of the Emerald Isle's noted saint was the occasion of a lavish expenditure of green ribbon, flags, etc.

Ertel & Houk have received a large supply of all kinds of garden seeds to furnish the million settlers around here.

Several large herds of antelope were seen here the last few days, likely attracted by the fact of some young travelling men stopping over. The antelope have lots of fun with the latter.

SADIE.
articles.summary: Belfield letter signed "Sadie": county organization, settlers, relinquishment speculation, an Indian horse-theft claim, St. Patrick's day and local doings.

articles.text: The effectual way in which the ice-dam, built last fall, protects the western bank of the river has called the attention of several to the fact that at a very trifling expense the channel could be turned so that the river will run as close to the abattoir as necessary. If this is done it will be a great benefit in two ways, in carrying away the debris from the abattoir and in saving the western bank, which threatens to wash away and dump several houses into the river. The matter will probably be attended to soon.
articles.summary: Suggests turning the river channel toward the abattoir, as last fall's ice-dam has protected the west bank.

articles.headline: Correspondence.
articles.text:
EDITOR COW BOY:

The recent effusion of a Dickinson correspondent in The Pioneer-Press prompts me to say a word in behalf of Belfield, which proudly looks to your aggressive journal as its champion, as long as it has not reached the stage where it can support a paper of its own.

Belfield possesses none of the "dog in the manger" element and congratulates Medora upon having scored "first blood" in the Black Hills freight-line contest. If its superior energy, unity of action, backed by the necessary cash, has secured for it a large share of this valuable freight, Belfield, who has made a gallant fight, cheerfully echos "amen." But what of Dickinson? Years before Belfield or Medora were dreamt of, Dickinson's wonderful advantages regarding the Black Hills freight route were or should have been known as well as now, and the very idea that its citizens should have permitted this fact, if such it be, to escape recognition augurs badly for a town, whose main brag is the imaginable halo surrounding the end of a freight division. Do the merchants of that hamlet, and they have some of the most wideawke in the country, begin to see that a few side tracks and a very modest freight-house are a mere myth, when it comes to the handling of fifty million pounds of freight? Would they grasp the idea that any village, even so humble, would gladly duplicate these accommodations for the terminus of a freight line and throw in a handsome bonus besides? Would they believe that the heavy freighters of the Hills are among the most intelligent, wide-awake men of the country, who are sure to select the shortest and best route where the hauling would be best, provided the rates of the railroad company would permit an option? Would Dickinson expect to come out victorious and carry off the trophies, when other towns, that happen to be blessed with better natural advantages, fight for it?

Dickinson is one of the most promising towns along the line, but it made a sad mistake when it allowed itself to be inflated with the erroneous idea that it could play a bluff game on other and younger places. Though its home journal had misled its own people by making them believe the freight line was theirs, the wail to the St. Paul Chamber of Commerce and The Pioneer-Press smacks too much of long clothes, and if no stronger efforts are put forth the freight line, as far as Dickinson is concerned, will remain and look best on paper.

In conclusion, Belfield trusts that Dickinson has not bankrupted itself in building stations and bridges, but if it has they will find ready purchasers for the same at Belfield, which will have use for them.

WORKER.
articles.summary: Letter from Belfield signed "Worker" congratulating Medora on winning the Black Hills freight contest and mocking Dickinson.

articles.headline: Correspondence.
articles.text:
LITTLE MISSOURI, March 20, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

In several German newspapers, The Extrablatt and The Mecklenberger Wachrichten, there is an article warning emigrants against the Northwest, especially Dakota. The writer of the article, Mr. Anton Milde, of Bismarck, seems to be entirely unacquainted with the country in which he is living. In his article he says that emigration speculators buy a section of land of 160 acres and lay it out in town lots, sell these as quick as possible and skip the country. Poor man, go to the U. S. land office and ask how many acres a section contains before you write another article.

Then he says that the winter is so severe, with continual lasting storms, that it is impossible to keep cattle except in heated stables. Where do people sometimes get the rage for writing about things they do not understand? If you would like to see cattle in winter-time, come out to the Bad Lands of Dakota and here you will find them neither stabled nor fed, but running free during the whole winter grazing.

Another sentence says nobody takes care of the emigrants after they are here, but have to seek their way alone to get enough to live on in winter. Well, let them bring wetnurses to lead these poor fellows who cannot find their way alone.

At the end of the article the writer wishing to prove his statements about Dakota says: "I will give an illustration of one case. A former Vienna lawyer, T. Kratky, has to make his living in New York by washing dishes in a restaurant." Old friend, what has your lawyer in New York to do with Dakota. Let him wash dishes. I hope he will do less damage than as a lawyer. The less lawyers there are the more peace there is in a place, and the less doctors and druggists the better the health of the people. This can be proved by Little Missouri, where there are no fights and only two children have died; they grow up as well or quick as calves.

To this ridiculous article of Mr. Anton Milde (in plain English Anton Softness) I can only reply that it is true both your article and your name are soft, much too soft for Dakota. Go East!

A.
articles.summary: Little Missouri letter signed "A." rebutting Anton Milde of Bismarck, who warned German emigrants against Dakota.
